title: Overflowing Glass Pyramid
statement:
Glasses are stacked in a pyramid: row 0 has one glass, row 1 has two, row i has i + 1. Glass j of row i rests on glasses j and j + 1 of row i + 1. Every glass holds exactly 1 unit.

You pour poured units into the top glass. When a glass is full, everything extra spills out split equally onto the two glasses below it. Glasses in the bottom rows that would spill just lose the extra.

Once everything has settled, return how full glass glass of row row is, as a number between 0 and 1 (rows and glasses are counted from 0). Answers within 10⁻⁵ are accepted.

examples.why: The top keeps 1 and spills 3, so each glass in row 1 gets 1.5 and spills 0.5. The middle glass of row 2 gets 0.25 from each side.
An edge glass has only one glass above it, so it fills half as fast as the middle one.
The top glass holds the single unit. Nothing spills.

hints: Instead of tracking how much each glass holds, track how much liquid flows through each glass in total.
If flow f reaches a glass, it keeps min(f, 1) and passes (f − 1) / 2 to each glass below when f > 1. Flow into a glass only comes from the row above.
Fill row by row: start with poured at the top and push the overflow of each glass into the next row. Stop at the requested row and cap the answer at 1.

explain.intuition:
Timing does not matter: whatever order the drops arrive in, a glass eventually receives some total amount and keeps at most 1 of it. So think of flow[i][j], the total amount that ever reaches glass (i, j). The top gets poured. Any glass with flow > 1 sends (flow − 1) / 2 down each side.

Each row depends only on the row above, so this is a small DP filled top to bottom, and one array for the current row is enough. The answer is min(1, flow[row][glass]). Note how quickly the edges starve: even 10⁹ units leave the edge glass of row 30 empty.
steps: For each row up to row − 1, create next with one more slot, filled with 0.
For each glass j in cur with cur[j] > 1, add (cur[j] − 1) / 2 to next[j] and next[j + 1].
Set cur = next. After reaching row, return min(1, cur[glass]).
pitfalls: Returning the flow without capping at 1. A glass never holds more than it can.
Passing the full flow down instead of only the excess above 1.
Splitting into three or into a single glass. Each glass feeds exactly j and j + 1 of the next row.

solutions.title: Full table of flows
solutions.idea: Fill a triangle of total flows row by row, pushing the excess of each glass into the two glasses below.

solutions.title: One row at a time
solutions.idea: Each row depends only on the row above, so keep just the current row.

followups: Find the smallest amount to pour so that a given glass becomes completely full.
Glasses now have different capacities. Does the row-by-row flow still work?
